name: Health center sites (permanent)
plain: How many permanent sites of community health centers are in each municipality. The list is from the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), a federal agency.
definition: Active sites in HRSA's list of Health Center Service Delivery and Look-Alike Sites that deliver care (their type is "Service Delivery Site" or "Administrative/Service Delivery Site") and whose location type is "Permanent", counted in the municipality that holds the site's county code. A federally funded health center (a Federally Qualified Health Center, FQHC) holds a federal health center grant; a look-alike meets the same requirements without the grant. Only sites whose status is "Active" are counted: HRSA uses that status for a site whose organization has a current health center grant and that is itself open for business. The Puerto Rico value is the sum of the 78 municipal values.
geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the sum of the 78 municipal values)

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, made from the HRSA files of 2026-10-06 (HRSA refreshes them daily). It is rebuilt with each full build (python health_series.py), and a later change at HRSA shows only after a rebuild.

method: health_series.py streams HRSA's file (all states and territories), keeps the Puerto Rico rows (Site State Abbreviation = PR) and seven of its columns, and counts, for each five-digit county code (the municipio), the rows whose status is Active, whose type delivers care and whose location type is Permanent. Of the 164 Puerto Rico rows in the 2026-11 snapshot, 120 are permanent sites that deliver care, 35 are mobile vans (health.hc_vans) and 9 are administrative-only buildings, which are left out. Names, addresses, telephone numbers, web addresses and coordinates are dropped as the file is read and are never stored or published.
source_detail: HRSA Data Warehouse, Health Center Service Delivery and Look-Alike Sites (CSV): columns Site State Abbreviation, Site Status Description, Health Center Type, Health Center Type Description, Health Center Location Type Description and State and County Federal Information Processing Standard Code.
how_to_read: Use it to see where the community health center sites are. In the 2026-11 snapshot San Juan has 7 permanent sites, Bayamón 7, and Mayagüez, Ponce, San Sebastián and Toa Alta 4 each; 8 municipalities have none (Añasco, Cataño, Fajardo, Guayanilla, Juana Díaz, Manatí, Sabana Grande and San Germán). On the Analysis tab the layer is shaded per 1,000 residents by default, so that a small municipality can be compared with a large one. A site is a place, not an organization, and not a measure of care: it says nothing about hours, services, staff or how many people a site serves.
caveats: HRSA lists only health centers that hold a federal grant or look-alike status. Hospitals, private clinics, doctors' offices and the island's own public health system are not in this file.
A zero is a real zero in HRSA's list. It does not mean residents have no care nearby: a site in the next municipality, a hospital or a private clinic can serve them.
A site belongs to the municipality HRSA gives for it, which is where the site is registered.

name: Health center mobile vans
plain: How many mobile health center vans are listed in each municipality. A van can work in other municipalities too. The list is from the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA).
definition: Active sites in HRSA's list of Health Center Service Delivery and Look-Alike Sites that deliver care and whose location type is "Mobile Van", counted in the municipality that holds the county code HRSA gives for the van. The Puerto Rico value is the sum of the 78 municipal values.
geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the sum of the 78 municipal values)

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, made from the HRSA files of 2026-10-06 (HRSA refreshes them daily). It is rebuilt with each full build (python health_series.py), and a later change at HRSA shows only after a rebuild.

method: Same file and same counting as health.hc_sites, for the rows whose location type is Mobile Van instead of Permanent. Administrative-only rows are left out, and names, addresses, telephone numbers, web addresses and coordinates are never stored or published.
source_detail: HRSA Data Warehouse, Health Center Service Delivery and Look-Alike Sites (CSV), column Health Center Location Type Description = Mobile Van.
how_to_read: In the 2026-11 snapshot HRSA lists 35 vans in 18 municipalities: Ponce has 6, Mayagüez 5, and Aguada and San Juan 3 each. Read each count as where the vans are listed, not as where they serve.
caveats: A van travels. HRSA gives one county for it, and this layer cannot follow it: a municipality with no van listed can still be served by a van listed elsewhere.
HRSA does not say how often or where a van works, so the count says nothing about service hours or reach.

name: Primary care physicians still needed, full-time equivalents (shortage areas)
plain: How many more primary care doctors a shortage area still needs for its federal shortage designation to end. The count is from the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), in full-time equivalents.
definition: The number of additional primary care physicians, in full-time equivalents (FTE), that HRSA says the municipality's designated primary care shortage area still needs for its ratio of people to practitioners to fall below the limit for designation, so that the designation would end. The limit is 3,500 people for each physician for a whole area, and 3,000 for a low-income population group or an area of unusually high need. HRSA's file states a goal of 3,000 to 1 for all 20 designations in Puerto Rico, and its figures work out to it. HRSA counts a practitioner's FTE by its own rules, which can count a practitioner as a fraction of an FTE or as none (its Shortage Designation Management System manual, August 2026). Only area-level designations count: the municipality's low-income residents, its whole population or a high-needs area (in the 2026-10 snapshot there are 20, one for each of 20 municipalities); facility designations (health centers, which HRSA designates by law, and a correctional facility) are left out. The Puerto Rico value adds the municipal values.
geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the sum of the 78 municipal values)

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, made from the HRSA files of 2026-10-06 (HRSA refreshes them daily). It is rebuilt with each full build (python health_series.py), and a later change at HRSA shows only after a rebuild.

method: health_series.py streams HRSA's primary care HPSA file (BCD_HPSA_FCT_DET_PC.csv, all states and territories), keeps the Puerto Rico rows and sixteen columns, and for each municipality takes the area-level designation whose status is Designated (or Proposed For Withdrawal, which HRSA still counts until the Federal Register notice) and whose type is Geographic HPSA, HPSA Population or High Needs Geographic HPSA. In the 2026-10 snapshot that gives 20 designations and 23 facility designations are left out. The value is the file's HPSA Shortage column. If a municipality ever had two area designations the build would keep the larger shortage (the groups overlap, so they are not added) and say so in the notes of the file; a designation that covers two municipalities stops the build. Check: HRSA's own Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary (as of 30 September 2026) gives 138 primary care practitioners needed for Puerto Rico; the sum of the municipal values is 135.2 and, with the correctional facility designation that HRSA includes, 136.8.
source_detail: HRSA Data Warehouse, Health Professional Shortage Area designations, primary care (BCD_HPSA_FCT_DET_PC.csv): columns HPSA Status, Designation Type, HPSA Shortage, Common State County FIPS Code and others.
how_to_read: Read it as the size of the gap in practitioners, not in people. In the 2026-10 snapshot the largest gaps are in San Juan (81.1), Río Grande (11.5), Toa Alta (6.4) and Arroyo (5.6); the smallest is 0.16. A large municipality needs more than a small one, so compare per 1,000 residents on the Analysis tab, or use the share of need met (health.hpsa_pc_met). 58 municipalities show no value.
caveats: No value (58 municipalities for primary care) means HRSA's file has no area-level primary care designation in force for the municipality. It is not a zero, not missing data and not proof that the municipality has enough doctors: for 57 of the 58 HRSA withdrew an area designation it once had, and 17 have only a facility designation (a health center or, in 1, a correctional facility).

San Juan's primary care designation has no practitioner in place (FTE 0) in HRSA's file, so its need met is 0% and its 81.1 practitioners still needed are 60% of the island's 135.2. That is how HRSA counts the physicians who serve the designated low-income residents, not a finding that no physician works in San Juan; read the island total and the map with it in mind.
HRSA's formula counts physicians only, not nurse practitioners or physician assistants. A municipality can have care that the formula does not see.

For a designation of a low-income population HRSA counts a practitioner's FTE from the time spent on low-income patients (Medicaid claims, or hours with Medicaid and sliding-fee patients), from hours that practitioners report in surveys run by the state primary care offices (HRSA's Shortage Designation Management System manual, August 2026): a practitioner who serves few such patients, or whose data HRSA does not have, adds little or nothing.

HRSA's practitioner counts belong to each designation and are as current as its last review: the primary care area designations in Puerto Rico were set between 2012 and 2023 and last updated between 2016 and 2023.
The Puerto Rico value adds the municipal values and leaves out the facility designations, so it is a little below HRSA's own total.

Per 1,000 residents, the Puerto Rico value divides the island's total by all of the island's residents, including those of the 58 municipalities with no designation (they add residents and no shortage), so it can be lower than the value of every municipality that has one.

name: Primary care physicians in place (% of the need)
plain: The share of the primary care doctors a shortage area needs that the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) counts as in place. It is not the share of people who get care.
definition: The primary care physicians in place (full-time equivalents) divided by the practitioners in place plus those still needed, times 100, for the municipality's area-level primary care designation. It is HRSA's "percent of need met" (HRSA divides the practitioners available by the number needed to bring the ratio of people to practitioners below the limit for designation), worked out here for each municipality from the file's HPSA FTE and HPSA Shortage columns. Only area-level designations count: the municipality's low-income residents, its whole population or a high-needs area (in the 2026-10 snapshot there are 20, one for each of 20 municipalities); facility designations (health centers, which HRSA designates by law, and a correctional facility) are left out. The Puerto Rico value is the sum of the municipal FTE divided by the sum of FTE plus shortage over the designated municipalities; it leaves out the facility designations that HRSA's own figure includes, so it reads 29.1% where HRSA's figure is 28.90%.
geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the summed practitioners in place divided by the summed practitioners needed, not an average of the municipal shares)

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, made from the HRSA files of 2026-10-06 (HRSA refreshes them daily). It is rebuilt with each full build (python health_series.py), and a later change at HRSA shows only after a rebuild.

method: Same designations as health.hpsa_pc_short. For each, need met = HPSA FTE ÷ (HPSA FTE + HPSA Shortage) × 100; there is no value when both are zero. Check against HRSA: adding the correctional facility designation to the 20 area designations gives 28.91%; HRSA's Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary (as of 30 September 2026) gives 28.90% for Puerto Rico. The populations also agree: the designation populations of the area designations (572,469) and the correctional facility (1,590) add up to HRSA's figure for the population of designated areas (574,059).
source_detail: HRSA Data Warehouse, Health Professional Shortage Area designations, primary care (BCD_HPSA_FCT_DET_PC.csv): columns HPSA FTE and HPSA Shortage; the definition of percent of need met is in the endnotes of HRSA's Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary.
how_to_read: 100% would end the designation; 0% means HRSA counts no physician for it. In the 2026-10 snapshot Maunabo (94.7%), Moca (94.7%) and Naguabo (94.6%) are the closest to ending their primary care designation, and 6 of the 20 designated municipalities are at 0% (Arroyo, Culebra, Maricao, Patillas, Río Grande and San Juan). Compare municipalities, not disciplines: each discipline has its own limit and its own designations.
caveats: It is the share of the practitioners that HRSA's formula needs and counts as in place. It is not the share of people who get care.

No value (58 municipalities for primary care) means HRSA's file has no area-level primary care designation in force for the municipality. It is not a zero, not missing data and not proof that the municipality has enough doctors: for 57 of the 58 HRSA withdrew an area designation it once had, and 17 have only a facility designation (a health center or, in 1, a correctional facility).

San Juan's primary care designation has no practitioner in place (FTE 0) in HRSA's file, so its need met is 0% and its 81.1 practitioners still needed are 60% of the island's 135.2. That is how HRSA counts the physicians who serve the designated low-income residents, not a finding that no physician works in San Juan; read the island total and the map with it in mind.

0% means HRSA counts no physician serving the designated population, not that none works in the municipality. For a designation of a low-income population HRSA counts a practitioner's FTE from the time spent on low-income patients (Medicaid claims, or hours with Medicaid and sliding-fee patients), from hours that practitioners report in surveys run by the state primary care offices (HRSA's Shortage Designation Management System manual, August 2026): a practitioner who serves few such patients, or whose data HRSA does not have, adds little or nothing.

HRSA's formula counts physicians only, not nurse practitioners or physician assistants. HRSA's practitioner counts belong to each designation and are as current as its last review: the primary care area designations in Puerto Rico were set between 2012 and 2023 and last updated between 2016 and 2023.
The share is the output of a federal formula. It is a good way to rank municipalities by how far each is from ending its designation, and a poor way to say how many people lack care.

name: Primary care shortage priority score
plain: A priority score that the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) gives a primary care shortage area. A higher score means a higher priority for sending National Health Service Corps (NHSC) clinicians.
definition: The HPSA Score of the municipality's area-level primary care designation: a whole number that HRSA's National Health Service Corps (NHSC), a federal program that places clinicians in shortage areas, uses to set priorities for assigning clinicians. HRSA scores primary care designations from 0 to 25 and says the higher the score, the greater the priority. HRSA builds the score by its own rules, so it is an index, not a measurement. plain: How many more psychiatrists a shortage area still needs, by the formula of the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), in full-time equivalents. HRSA's formula asks for more psychiatrists than the goal HRSA states for these areas.
definition: The number of additional psychiatrists (the one kind of practitioner that every mental health designation of Puerto Rico counts), in full-time equivalents (FTE), that HRSA says the municipality's designated mental health shortage area still needs to bring its ratio of people to practitioners down to the ratio HRSA works the figure out against. The rules set the limit for designating a whole area at 30,000 people for each psychiatrist and, for a low-income population group or an area of unusually high need, at 20,000 for each psychiatrist or at 15,000 together with 4,500 for each core mental health professional (42 CFR Part 5, Appendix C). At 20,000 the 52 designations would need about 50.5 psychiatrists, not 69.5. The observatory publishes HRSA's figure as HRSA gives it. HRSA counts a practitioner's FTE by its own rules, which can count a practitioner as a fraction of an FTE or as none (its Shortage Designation Management System manual, August 2026). how_to_read: Read it as the size of the gap in practitioners, not in people. In the 2026-10 snapshot the largest gaps are in Aguadilla (2.6), Humacao (2.5), Trujillo Alto (2.4) and Cabo Rojo (2.4); the smallest is 0.38. A large municipality needs more than a small one, so compare per 1,000 residents on the Analysis tab, or use the share of need met (health.hpsa_mh_met). 26 municipalities show no value.
caveats: No value (26 municipalities for mental health) means HRSA's file has no area-level mental health designation in force for the municipality. It is not a zero, not missing data and not proof that the municipality has enough psychiatrists or mental health care: for all 26 HRSA withdrew an area designation it once had, and 11 have only a facility designation (a health center or, in 1, a correctional facility).

HRSA's formula counts psychiatrists only: every one of the area designations in Puerto Rico is based on psychiatrists alone, so psychologists, clinical social workers and other mental health providers are not counted. A municipality can have care that the formula does not see.

For a designation of a low-income population HRSA counts a practitioner's FTE from the time spent on low-income patients (Medicaid claims, or hours with Medicaid and sliding-fee patients), from hours that practitioners report in surveys run by the state primary care offices (HRSA's Shortage Designation Management System manual, August 2026): a practitioner who serves few such patients, or whose data HRSA does not have, adds little or nothing.

HRSA's practitioner counts belong to each designation and are as current as its last review: the mental health area designations in Puerto Rico were set between 2022 and 2024 and last updated between 2022 and 2024.
The Puerto Rico value adds the municipal values and leaves out the facility designations, so it is a little below HRSA's own total.

Per 1,000 residents, the Puerto Rico value divides the island's total by all of the island's residents, including those of the 26 municipalities with no designation (they add residents and no shortage), so it can be lower than the value of every municipality that has one.

name: Psychiatrists in place (% of the need)
plain: The share of the psychiatrists a shortage area needs, by the formula of the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), that HRSA counts as in place. It is not the share of people who get care.
definition: The mental health providers (in Puerto Rico, psychiatrists) in place (full-time equivalents) divided by the practitioners in place plus those still needed, times 100, for the municipality's area-level mental health designation. It is HRSA's "percent of need met" (HRSA divides the practitioners available by the number needed to bring the ratio of people to practitioners below the limit for designation), worked out here for each municipality from the file's HPSA FTE and HPSA Shortage columns. Only area-level designations count: the municipality's low-income residents, its whole population or a high-needs area (in the 2026-10 snapshot there are 52, one for each of 52 municipalities); facility designations (health centers, which HRSA designates by law, and a correctional facility) are left out. The Puerto Rico value is the sum of the municipal FTE divided by the sum of FTE plus shortage over the designated municipalities; it leaves out the facility designations that HRSA's own figure includes, so it reads 8.5% where HRSA's figure is 8.31%.
geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the summed practitioners in place divided by the summed practitioners needed, not an average of the municipal shares)

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, made from the HRSA files of 2026-10-06 (HRSA refreshes them daily). It is rebuilt with each full build (python health_series.py), and a later change at HRSA shows only after a rebuild.

method: Same designations as health.hpsa_mh_short. For each, need met = HPSA FTE ÷ (HPSA FTE + HPSA Shortage) × 100; there is no value when both are zero. Check against HRSA: adding the correctional facility designation to the 52 area designations gives 8.32%; HRSA's Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary (as of 30 September 2026) gives 8.31% for Puerto Rico. The populations also agree: the designation populations of the area designations (1,138,425) and the correctional facility (2,500) add up to HRSA's figure for the population of designated areas (1,140,925).
source_detail: HRSA Data Warehouse, Health Professional Shortage Area designations, mental health (BCD_HPSA_FCT_DET_MH.csv): columns HPSA FTE and HPSA Shortage; the definition of percent of need met is in the endnotes of HRSA's Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary.
how_to_read: 100% would end the designation; 0% means HRSA counts no provider for it. In the 2026-10 snapshot Yabucoa (55.9%), Coamo (51.8%) and Guayama (49.1%) are the closest to ending their mental health designation, and 44 of the 52 designated municipalities are at 0% (Adjuntas, Aguada, Aguadilla and Aguas Buenas and others). Compare municipalities, not disciplines: each discipline has its own limit and its own designations.
caveats: It is the share of the practitioners that HRSA's formula needs and counts as in place. It is not the share of people who get care.

No value (26 municipalities for mental health) means HRSA's file has no area-level mental health designation in force for the municipality. It is not a zero, not missing data and not proof that the municipality has enough psychiatrists or mental health care: for all 26 HRSA withdrew an area designation it once had, and 11 have only a facility designation (a health center or, in 1, a correctional facility).

0% means HRSA counts no provider serving the designated population, not that none works in the municipality. For a designation of a low-income population HRSA counts a practitioner's FTE from the time spent on low-income patients (Medicaid claims, or hours with Medicaid and sliding-fee patients), from hours that practitioners report in surveys run by the state primary care offices (HRSA's Shortage Designation Management System manual, August 2026): a practitioner who serves few such patients, or whose data HRSA does not have, adds little or nothing.

HRSA's formula counts psychiatrists only: every one of the area designations in Puerto Rico is based on psychiatrists alone, so psychologists, clinical social workers and other mental health providers are not counted. HRSA's practitioner counts belong to each designation and are as current as its last review: the mental health area designations in Puerto Rico were set between 2022 and 2024 and last updated between 2022 and 2024.
The share is the output of a federal formula. It is a good way to rank municipalities by how far each is from ending its designation, and a poor way to say how many people lack care.

name: Mental health shortage priority score
plain: A priority score that the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) gives a mental health shortage area. A higher score means a higher priority for sending National Health Service Corps (NHSC) clinicians.
definition: The HPSA Score of the municipality's area-level mental health designation: a whole number that HRSA's National Health Service Corps (NHSC), a federal program that places clinicians in shortage areas, uses to set priorities for assigning clinicians. HRSA scores mental health designations from 0 to 25 and says the higher the score, the greater the priority. HRSA builds the score by its own rules, so it is an index, not a measurement. Only area-level designations count: the municipality's low-income residents, its whole population or a high-needs area (in the 2026-10 snapshot there are 52, one for each of 52 municipalities); facility designations (health centers, which HRSA designates by law, and a correctional facility) are left out. If a municipality had more than one area designation the highest score would be shown. There is no value for Puerto Rico as a whole because scores are not added or averaged.
geography: 78 municipalities (no value for Puerto Rico as a whole)

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, made from the HRSA files of 2026-10-06 (HRSA refreshes them daily). It is rebuilt with each full build (python health_series.py), and a later change at HRSA shows only after a rebuild.

method: Same designations as health.hpsa_mh_short; the value is the file's HPSA Score column, as a whole number.
source_detail: HRSA Data Warehouse, Health Professional Shortage Area designations, mental health (BCD_HPSA_FCT_DET_MH.csv): column HPSA Score.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot the mental health scores of the 52 designated municipalities run from 11 to 23; Guánica, Guayanilla and Jayuya and 1 more have the highest (23). Use it to rank municipalities within one discipline. Scores of different disciplines (primary care, dental, mental health) come from different rules and different designations, so they are not on one scale.
caveats: No value (26 municipalities for mental health) means HRSA's file has no area-level mental health designation in force for the municipality. It is not a zero, not missing data and not proof that the municipality has enough psychiatrists or mental health care: for all 26 HRSA withdrew an area designation it once had, and 11 have only a facility designation (a health center or, in 1, a correctional facility).
A score ranks priority for clinician placement. It does not measure how many people lack care, and it can change when HRSA reviews the designation.

HRSA's practitioner counts belong to each designation and are as current as its last review: the mental health area designations in Puerto Rico were set between 2022 and 2024 and last updated between 2022 and 2024.

name: How health center sites are counted (HRSA)
plain: The sites come from the public list of the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) of health centers with a federal grant or look-alike status (a look-alike meets the same rules without the grant). The observatory counts permanent sites that deliver care, counts mobile vans apart and publishes only the counts.
definition: HRSA's Health Center Service Delivery and Look-Alike Sites file lists each site of a health center that holds a federal Health Center Program grant (FQHC) or look-alike status, with the county that holds the site. A site's status says whether its organization holds a current grant and the site is open; its type says whether it offers direct patient care, works as an administrative office or both; its location type says whether it is permanent, a mobile van, seasonal or unknown.
geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the sum of the 78 municipal values)

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, made from the HRSA files of 2026-10-06 (HRSA refreshes them daily). It is rebuilt with each full build (python health_series.py), and a later change at HRSA shows only after a rebuild.

method: (1) health_series.py downloads the file once and streams it, so the whole file is never held. (2) It keeps the rows whose Site State Abbreviation is PR and seven columns: state, status, health center type, site type, location type, the five-digit county code and the record date; names, addresses, telephone numbers, web addresses and coordinates are dropped as each row is read, so they never reach the cache. (3) A row counts when its status is Active and its type contains "Service Delivery" (a service delivery site, or an administrative and service delivery site). (4) Permanent rows are counted as hc_sites and Mobile Van rows as hc_vans, for each county code that is one of the 78 municipios; a county code that is not one stops the build. (5) A municipality with no row has a count of zero, and the Puerto Rico value is the sum.
how_to_read: A count is the number of places HRSA lists, not the number of clinics (one organization can run many sites) or the number of people served. HRSA says that, for domestic violence shelters, the building number, street and ZIP Code are removed; the observatory drops every address as each row is read, before anything is saved. The file does not say which sites accept which patients or what services they offer.
caveats: The list covers only health centers in HRSA's Health Center Program. It leaves out hospitals, private practices and the island's public health facilities.
The county code is the one HRSA registers for the site; a site on a municipal boundary is counted once, in that municipality.

name: How shortage areas, practitioners needed and need met are read (HRSA)
plain: A Health Professional Shortage Area is a federal label, called a designation, for an area, a group of people or a facility with too few primary care, dental or mental health practitioners. The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) gives it. The observatory shows, for each municipality, the priority score, the practitioners still needed and the share of need met.
definition: HRSA designates a Health Professional Shortage Area (HPSA) when the ratio of people to practitioners passes a limit (for primary care, 3,500 to 1 for a whole area and 3,000 to 1 for a low-income population group or an area of unusually high need; for dental care, 5,000 to 1 and 4,000 to 1; for mental health, based on psychiatrists, 30,000 to 1 for a whole area and, for a low-income population group or an area of unusually high need, 20,000 to 1 or 15,000 to 1 together with 4,500 to 1 for core mental health professionals; HRSA's file states a goal of 3,000, 4,000 and 20,000 to 1 for the primary care, dental and mental health designations of Puerto Rico, and its mental health figures work out at about 15,000). A designation covers a geographic area, a population group or a facility. HRSA's "practitioners needed to remove designations" is the number of additional practitioners that its formula says would bring the ratio down to its target, and its "percent of need met" is the practitioners in place divided by the number that formula needs.
geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the sum of the 78 municipal values)

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, made from the HRSA files of 2026-10-06 (HRSA refreshes them daily). It is rebuilt with each full build (python health_series.py), and a later change at HRSA shows only after a rebuild.

method: (1) health_series.py downloads HRSA's three files (primary care, dental health, mental health) once and streams them, keeping the Puerto Rico rows and sixteen columns without names. (2) It keeps a designation when its status is Designated or Proposed For Withdrawal (HRSA counts both) and its type is Geographic HPSA, HPSA Population or High Needs Geographic HPSA: the area-level designations. Facility designations (health centers designated by law, and one correctional facility) are left out of the municipal values. (3) A designation is assigned to the municipality of its county code; it must be the only row of its HPSA ID (one that covered two municipalities would stop the build). (4) For a municipality the score is the highest HPSA Score, the practitioners still needed is HPSA Shortage, and need met is HPSA FTE ÷ (HPSA FTE + HPSA Shortage) × 100. If a municipality ever had two area designations the larger shortage would be kept, because the groups overlap, and the file's notes would count it. (5) A municipality with no area-level designation has no value, never a zero. (6) The Puerto Rico value is the sum of the shortages and the ratio of the summed FTE to the summed FTE plus shortage; scores have no Puerto Rico value. Check against HRSA: its Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary (as of 30 September 2026) gives, for Puerto Rico, 138, 297 and 70 practitioners needed and 28.90%, 48.02% and 8.31% of need met for primary care, dental health and mental health. With the correctional facility designation added to the municipal ones, the build gets 136.8, 298.4 and 70.7 practitioners (each within 1.1%) and 28.91%, 48.02% and 8.32%, and the designation populations add up exactly to HRSA's (574,059; 2,292,005; 1,140,925).
how_to_read: In Puerto Rico every area-level designation read here is for a low-income population group (one dental designation is a high-needs geographic area), so the figures describe the shortage for those residents, as HRSA measures it, and not for every resident. Compare municipalities within one discipline. The score ranks priority, the practitioners still needed measures the gap and the share of need met shows how far a municipality is from ending its designation.
caveats: HRSA's formulas count primary care physicians only (not nurse practitioners or physician assistants), dentists only, and, for every mental health designation in Puerto Rico, psychiatrists only.
Designations are reviewed on HRSA's schedule: the area designations read here were set between 2012 and 2024 and last updated between 2016 and 2024, so a figure can be years behind the present.

The Medically Underserved Area (MUA/P) file is not used: its 72 Puerto Rico rows are all from 1978, and the underservice score, which HRSA builds from four indicators that are empty in those rows, reads 0.00 for 71 of them and 50.00 for one. The Area Health Resources File is not used because its documentation does not authorize re-use without the Bureau's permission.
